package_info.why_malicious: This package is a highly targeted supply chain attack leveraging dependency confusion. It executes a malicious postinstall script that exfiltrates host and environment information via DNS, attempts to access private registry credentials, downloads and replaces itself with a private version, exfiltrates sensitive files, and finally deploys a C2 agent capable of arbitrary code execution, file exfiltration, and system traversal. The package is designed to evade detection, clean up after itself, and maintain persistence for remote control.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the postinstall script executes confsettingsaaa.js, launching the first stage of the malware, which initiates environment reconnaissance and sets up further malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Postinstall scripts that invoke non-standard or obfuscated files are a common initial vector for malware, as they execute automatically during package installation without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely require postinstall scripts unless for build or setup purposes; in this case, it is used to launch obfuscated code unrelated to normal package setup.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some packages use postinstall for compiling native modules or performing legitimate setup tasks, but not for launching obfuscated or unrelated scripts.
key_indicators: Postinstall script invoking a non-standard, obfuscated JavaScript file
No legitimate reason for postinstall in this context
Script name (confsettingsaaa.js) does not match standard naming conventions

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code performs DNS lookups that encode the username, hostname, package name, and NO_PROXY environment variable as subdomains to an attacker-controlled domain, covertly exfiltrating reconnaissance data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating system and environment information via DNS queries is a covert data theft technique that can bypass traditional network monitoring.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not exfiltrate host or environment data, especially not by encoding it in DNS queries to external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, telemetry or analytics might use DNS for basic checks, but not for transmitting sensitive or identifying data.
key_indicators: DNS lookups to attacker-controlled domain with encoded sensitive data
Encoding of username, hostname, package name, and environment variables in DNS queries
Use of process.env and os modules to gather host information

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On error or if certain conditions are not met during installation, the code deletes its own files, creates decoy package.json and index.js files with a misleading message, and terminates the process, performing anti-forensics and deception.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-deletion and decoy file creation are classic anti-forensics and evasion tactics designed to hinder analysis and mislead investigators.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not delete their own files or replace them with misleading placeholders to cover up malicious activity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some uninstallers clean up files, but not in a deceptive manner that creates misleading decoy files.
key_indicators: Deletes own files on error or failed checks
Creates decoy package.json and index.js with misleading messages
Terminates process after cleanup to prevent further analysis

execution_context.trigger: postinstall (if .npmrc with private registry credentials is found)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, if private registry credentials are detected, the code downloads a private package variant, installs it in a subdirectory, replaces the current package, exfiltrates sensitive files (package.json, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf) via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled server, decrypts and launches a second-stage agent, then cleans up and exits.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Conditional logic to target only environments with private registry credentials, exfiltration of sensitive files, and deployment of a second-stage agent are hallmarks of advanced targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not replace themselves, exfiltrate system files, or launch hidden agents based on the presence of private credentials.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case exists for this combination of behaviors; this is highly targeted and malicious.
key_indicators: Checks for private registry credentials in .npmrc
Downloads and installs private package variant
Exfiltrates /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and package.json via HTTPS POST
Decrypts and launches hidden second-stage agent

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the second-stage agent is launched, the code registers with the C2 server, receives encryption keys and a UUID, collects detailed system and environment information, encrypts it, and exfiltrates it via HTTPS POST to the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: C2 registration and encrypted exfiltration of host details are classic remote access trojan (RAT) behaviors, enabling persistent remote control and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code does not register with external C2 servers or send encrypted host data to unknown endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate package should perform C2 registration or exfiltrate encrypted system information.
key_indicators: C2 registration via HTTPS POST to external server
Encrypted exfiltration of host and environment data
Collection of detailed system and environment information

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the agent enters a command loop, receiving instructions from the C2 server to execute arbitrary code, exfiltrate or download files, or delete itself, enabling full remote control and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote code execution and file exfiltration on command are core RAT features, providing attackers with persistent and flexible control over the compromised system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should allow remote arbitrary code execution, file exfiltration, or self-deletion based on external commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case exists for this behavior in npm packages.
key_indicators: Supports exec/eval commands from C2 server
File upload/download on demand from remote server
Self-deletion capability triggered by C2 command

attack_chain.action: Postinstall script executes obfuscated wrapper (confsettingsaaa.js) on install.
Reconnaissance: Exfiltrates username, hostname, package name, and NO_PROXY via DNS to attacker-controlled domain.
Searches for .npmrc/private registry credentials; if not found, invokes fail function to self-delete and create decoy files.
If private registry credentials are found, downloads and installs private package, replaces itself, exfiltrates sensitive files, and launches second-stage agent.
Second-stage agent registers with C2, exfiltrates detailed system info, and enters command loop.
Agent receives and executes C2 commands: arbitrary code execution, file exfiltration, system traversal, or self-deletion.

behavioral_signatures: Postinstall script invoking obfuscated or non-standard JavaScript files (e.g., confsettingsaaa.js)
DNS lookups encoding host, user, package, or environment data to external domains controlled by the attacker
Conditional logic to check for private registry credentials in .npmrc and self-delete if not found
Exfiltration of /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and package.json via HTTPS POST to attacker-controlled domains
Decryption and execution of hidden second-stage agent (obfusc.dec.js)
Agent registering with external C2 and supporting remote code execution, file exfiltration, and self-deletion
file_indicators: Decoy package.json and index.js with message: 'Please refer to the private registry instead of the public repo; Security Team'
.documentation/ (temporary install directory for private package variant)
Presence of ldtzstxwzpntxqn and lznfjbhurpjsqmr as dependencies
network_indicators: DNS queries to *.pkgio.com or similar attacker-controlled domains with encoded host/user/environment data
HTTPS POST requests to https://www.pkgio.com/ and related endpoints
C2 registration and communication to attacker-controlled IPs (e.g., DigitalOcean hosted)
POST requests to /register and /updateinfosnodejs endpoints on C2 infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with postinstall scripts invoking obfuscated or non-standard files such as confsettingsaaa.js. Flag DNS queries that encode host, user, or environment data to external domains like *.pkgio.com. Detect exfiltration of system files (e.g., /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, package.json) via HTTPS POST to unknown or attacker-controlled domains. Look for the presence of decoy package.json and index.js files with suspicious messages. Monitor for processes that decrypt and execute hidden JavaScript agents (obfusc.dec.js), and for outbound connections to known C2 endpoints or domains associated with pkgio.com. Correlate the presence of suspicious dependencies (ldtzstxwzpntxqn, lznfjbhurpjsqmr) with these behaviors to identify targeted supply chain attacks.
